newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: DOWNER SAYS AID ISSUE SHOULD BE DISCUSSED BY INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY
The Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer, says it is unlikely Australia will cut its level of foreign aid to Cambodia.
Mr Downer said Australia will discuss its $32 million in aid to Cambodia during talks with Japan, America and Europe, for a co-ordinated response on aid.
But Mr Downer said aid would continue at its present level for now.
The Minister says Australia is consulting with other aid donors about the issues of aid.
Mr Downer says it would make more sense for the international community to discuss the issue of aid to Cambodia together.
FEDERAL POLICE SUPPORT CALLS FOR IMPLOSION MORATORIUM
Federal Police have supported calls for national moratorium on the implosion of derelict buildings.
It follows the death of a 12-year-old girl yesterday who was among spectators showered with debris at the demolition of former hospital buildings in Canberra.
ACT Chief Minister Kate Carnell says all States and Territory Governments have been urged to halt building implosions until Australian safety standards are reviewed.
Federal Police Assistant Commissioner Bill Stoll supports the move.
Meanwhile, Mrs Carnell has accused the construction industry union of trying to politicise the tragedy.
C.F.M.E.U. Branch Secretary George Wasson is calling on Mrs Carnell to stand aside pending an inquiry.
He says the Chief Minister intervened in the tender process to ensure implosion was selected as the preferred method of demolition.

Mrs Carnell says she is confident the Coroner's inquiry, police investigations, and the independent inquiry to be headed by a former Commonwealth bureaucrat, will prove the tender process was carried out correctly.
HOWARD OFFERS SYMPATHY TO FAMILY OF DEMOLITION VICTIM
The Prime Minister has extended his sympathy to the family of the 12-year-old girl who was killed during yesterday's demolition.
John Howard says the accident was not only tragic but it was also an extraordinarily unsettling event given the community focus of the event.
He says the Federal Government will co-operate with the inquiry set up by the ACT Government.
The Prime Minister says he believes the ACT Government has acted properly and correctly in covering all the necessary contingencies in calling for an inquiry.

Mr Howard says he wishes a speedy recovery to good health to those still in hospital, and expressed his and the Government's sympathy to the family of the young girl who lost her life in the accident.
BHP CONFIDENT NUMBER ONE DISPUTE WILL NOT WIDEN
BHP is confident the Rio Tinto contract dispute in the New South Wales Hunter Valley, will not spread inter-State to its 9 mines in the coal rich Bowen-Basin in Central Queensland.
ACTU boss Jenny George has alarmed Queensland coal mining companies by indicating the 32 day dispute at the Hunter Valley Number One mine could widen.
But, BHP's Ian Dymock, says the company has an industrial agreement with its employees, that will keep the dispute out of its Bowen Basin coal mines.
Mr Dymock says part of the agreement with the unions is to avoid involvement in disputes that are external.
He believes BHP does not believe the current New South Wales dispute will widen.
LECTURER BELIEVES HANSON SUPPORT A RETURN TO NATIONALISM
A Policy Sciences Lecturer has warned that Pauline Hanson's One Nation Party has a good chance of winning seats in the Senate, and may top the primary votes of the Greens and Democrats.
Lance McMahon, of Perth's Curtin University, says Senators Harradine and Colston have shown the power that can be exercised over Government by the casting of their votes on key issues.
Mr McMahon says strong leadership is needed to marginalise Australia's Far Right, and to clearly communicate Australia's desire for continued engagement in Asia.
He says the Federal Government appears to have been unable to grasp the fact that the support for Pauline Hanson is a return to the heart of Australian nationalism.
Mr McMahon believes this point has been overlooked.

He says despite Gough Whitlam saying in 1974, "the White Australia's Policy's dead, give me a shovel and I'll bury it", there is clearly still a strong sentiment in the Australian electorate for those policies.
MINISTER SAYS TESTS DELAY TO BLAME FOR DELAY IN IMPORTS DECISION
Federal Primary Industries Minister John Anderson says there has been a delay in tests to determine whether Australia should import cooked chicken meat.
Australia is under pressure from suppliers in the United States, Canada and Thailand to allow cooked chicken meat imports.
But Australian quarantine authorities and chicken growers are concerned about the risk of imported bird diseases, including Newcastle Disease.
Mr Anderson says he is hoping for the results soon.
The Minister says the Government has sent the issue on for further testing to the world's leading avarian specialist in the United Kingdom.

Mr Anderson: "that work is taking an inordinate amount of time to be completed. I gather they've had some domestic problems in the UK, but I must say it would be very nice to have those results back so that we know one way or another exactly where we're going."
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
